summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator compares two landing scenarios on the Moon. You give it two sites on the same date, or one site on two dates, and it tells you which one loses the Sun or the Earth first and by how long.

We built it because mission schedules slip and landing sites get moved. Near the south pole the Sun and the Earth both sit within a few degrees of the horizon, and the horizon is ridges and crater rims. A two-week delay, or a site 175 km away, can leave a lander without power or without a direct radio link for days. JPL Horizons, Quickmap and Moon Trek hold the data to check this, one site and one date at a time. Our tool puts two cases side by side.

For each scenario the tool works out where the Sun and the Earth sit above the real skyline, how long each stays in view, and how much solar energy arrives. The skyline comes from NASA's LOLA laser altimeter grids. In a 90-day run the rim of Shackleton crater gets sunlight 91% of the time and the crater floor 10 km away gets none. We tested the Sun and Earth positions against NASA JPL Horizons, and the largest difference we found was 0.0073 degrees.

The tool also maps a year of sunlight around the south pole from the same terrain. The sunniest point on our map gets sunlight 90.9% of the year. It is 136 m from the place a published study of LOLA data gives as the best-lit at the south pole (Mazarico and others, 2011).
details:
What it does

You choose scenario A and scenario B. Each one is a place on the Moon and a start time. You can pick the place from a list, type a latitude and longitude, or click the 3D Moon. The list has six landing sites with sourced coordinates (IM-1 Odysseus, the planned IM-2 site, the Blue Ghost Mission 1 landing region, Apollo 11, 15 and 17) and two reference points at Shackleton crater.

The page then shows both scenarios together:

  • A sentence at the top with the result, for example "B loses sight of the Earth in 9 d. A keeps it for at least the next 90 days."
  • A table of numbers for a look-ahead period of 3, 14, 30 or 90 days. It gives the height and compass direction of the Sun and the Earth at the start, the time to the next sunset and Earthset, hours of sunlight, solar energy in kWh per square metre, hours with the Earth in view, and the longest stretch without each.
  • A view out from each site. The ground is drawn as the real skyline, with the paths of the Sun and the Earth crossing it.
  • A timeline of height above the skyline for the whole period, with bars that show when the Sun and the Earth are up.
  • A 3D Moon with both sites marked, lit from the Sun's real direction. Play runs the period forward. You can drag the Moon to turn it or click it to move a site.
  • A Horizon control that switches between the LOLA skyline and a flat horizon, so you can see how much of an answer comes from terrain.
  • A Sunlight map button. It colours the ground within 6 degrees of the south pole by the share of a year each spot spends in sunlight, and marks the five sunniest places. One click puts a scenario on any of them.

Four worked cases load with one click:

  • Move the site 175 km. From the IM-1 landing site the Earth stays in view for all 90 days. From the planned IM-2 site it sets after 9 days, and the longest stretch without it is 5 d 17 h. The IM-2 site gets more sunlight, 1,389 kWh per square metre against 1,164.
  • Land two weeks late at the IM-1 site. A lander that arrives on landing day gets 8 d 15 h before the Sun goes behind the ridges. One that arrives 14 days later lands in the dark and waits 12 d 2 h for sunrise.
  • Compare the rim of Shackleton crater with its floor, about 10 km apart at the south pole. Over 90 days the rim is in sunlight 91% of the time and the floor gets none. With a flat horizon the tool gives 53% and 47%.
  • Set the pole beside Apollo 11. At the Apollo 11 site the Sun is 86° up. At the IM-1 site it clears the skyline by 10.3°, and the Earth sits between 2.5° and 16.4° above it.

The address bar holds the whole comparison, so you can copy the link and send someone the exact case you are looking at.

The site also has a page called "Our thinking". It explains the choices we made and follows one comparison from its inputs to the sentence on screen.

Who it is for

Mission planners who need a first answer when a date or a site changes, before a full terrain study. It also works for teachers and students who want to see why the south pole is a hard place to land.

How it works

The page is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework and no server. It opens from a file and works offline. Astronomy Engine supplies the positions of the Sun, the Earth and the Moon, and the IAU 2009 rotation model gives the Moon's orientation. Our code turns those into a height and a compass direction for someone standing at the site.

Within 17 degrees of either pole, the horizon is a skyline worked out from NASA's LOLA polar elevation grids (LDEM_60S_240M and LDEM_60N_240M). For each of 720 compass directions we find the highest ground out to 200 km, as seen from 2 m above the surface. The polar sites in the list use the full 240 m grid, computed ahead of time. Any other polar point uses a 960 m grid and is computed in the browser in about 20 milliseconds. The Sun or the Earth counts as up when it is higher than the ground in its direction. Farther from the poles we use a flat horizon, because the Sun crosses it steeply there and a 2 degree ridge shifts sunrise by about 4 hours.

Solar energy is the sunlight that reaches one square metre facing the Sun. We start from 1,361 W per square metre at the Earth's distance from the Sun, adjust for the Sun's distance that day, and count the share of the Sun's disk above the skyline.

The 3D Moon is WebGL code written for this project, with no library behind it. It shades a sphere using the NASA colour mosaic and ground slopes worked out from the laser altimeter heights.

The sunlight map is made ahead of time by a Python script. It splits the ground poleward of 84 degrees south into 50,220 cells of 1.44 km, finds the skyline at the highest point of each from the 240 m grid, and checks the Sun against it every hour for a year from Nov 15, 2026. The page draws the result on the 3D Moon.

How we know the numbers are right

Positions. Our tests compare the tool with tables saved from NASA JPL Horizons, 852 time steps at four places on the Moon. The largest difference in Sun or Earth position is 0.0073 degrees. With a flat horizon, the sunset time at the IM-1 site is 4 seconds from the Horizons time. We also test the Sun direction that lights the 3D Moon over another 278 time steps, where the largest difference is 0.0067 degrees.

Terrain. On made-up terrain where we know the answer (flat ground, a wall, a bowl), the skyline code gives that answer. On the real grid it agrees with a second version written in Python within 0.05 degrees, over 2,160 directions at three sites. The grid puts the IM-1 site at 2,588 m, and NASA gives 2,579 m. The floor of Shackleton crater is in permanent shadow, and it gets no sunlight in the tool. Mazarico and others (2011) report a point near the Shackleton rim that is sunlit for most of the year. Our rim point gets sunlight 87% of the time over 2024.

Sunlight map. The sunniest point on the map is at 89.45 S, 222.69 E. Mazarico and others (2011) give the same coordinates for the best-lit place they found at the south pole, and our point is 136 m from theirs. The figures published for it, over about 20 years, are 89.0% average illumination and 141 hours for the longest time in shadow. Ours for one year are 90.4% and 143 hours. We made the comparison after the map was finished. The page's own code, run on the map's five sunniest points, gives the map's yearly figure within half a percentage point at each.

All 44 tests run with one command, node --test, and need nothing installed.

What it leaves out

We use terrain within 17 degrees of a pole and a flat horizon elsewhere. The 240 m and 960 m grids smooth narrow ridges and small craters. At the IM-1 site the two grids put the first sunset 4 hours apart, and on a narrow peak the coarse grid can miss about a quarter of the year's sunlight. We treat the lander as a point 2 m above the ground with no tilt. The sunlight map covers the south pole only, for one year, on cells 1.44 km wide.

The energy figure is sunlight arriving, before any panel turns it into electricity. We don't model panel angle, efficiency, temperature or dust. "Earth in view" means the centre of the Earth's disk is above the skyline, and we don't model an antenna, a ground station or a data rate. The page states these limits next to the numbers. The 3D Moon is a picture, and the numbers are calculated separately from it.

What comes next

NASA Goddard publishes 5 m LOLA grids for south pole landing sites, and adding them would resolve the nearest ridges. After that we would add solar panel tilt and an antenna model. We would also like to add landing sites from other countries' lunar programs.

Tools

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, WebGL 2, Node.js test runner, Python with NumPy and Pillow for the data scripts, Astronomy Engine 2.1.19, Mona Sans typeface.

Source code

https://github.com/PuggLord/lunar-landing-site-navigator. License: MIT.

How we used AI

We used one AI coding tool, Claude Code (Anthropic, model Claude Fable 5.2).

The idea is ours: pick a landing site and a time, see where the Sun and the Earth are, and compare two scenarios. Comparing sites and dates comes from the challenge statement.

Jake Manis ran the sessions with the tool. What the team decided:

  • The challenge, and the idea of comparing two scenarios side by side.
  • To make a new build during the event.
  • That the first design looked machine-made, and that the page should be rebuilt from published design references.
  • Which past Space Apps winners to study before writing the slides.
  • What to deliver: the live tool, seven slides, a short video and this page.
  • To ask where the project could lose, and then to add the terrain skyline and the energy figure in answer.
  • That the first drafts of the text read as machine-written, that they should be rewritten in plain language, and that the site needed a page explaining our thinking.
  • To put the script on screen in the video, and that the first script did not sound like us and had to be rewritten. We meant to read it aloud and did not record the voices in time, so the video has no sound.
  • To make the code public under the MIT license, and to use the 30-second video as the demo.
  • To ask for one feature a judge would remember. The tool proposed the sunlight map and built it, and we chose to keep it.

The checks on the numbers are automated tests. The tool wrote them and ran them, and reported the results to us.

We directed the tool as it wrote the code, the tests, the documentation, the slides and the first draft of this page. The tool read the Space Apps guides and downloaded reference tables from NASA JPL Horizons. It downloaded and converted NASA's Moon maps and LOLA elevation grids, and it looked at published websites for design reference. A web capture service, Firecrawl, took screenshots of those reference sites and read three NASA pages, one paper abstract and one preprint.

How we label it. Each AI-written file starts with an "SI disclosure" comment, and the pages and the slides carry a generator tag in their metadata. The file SI_USE.md in the repository logs each session with times and files.

The project has no AI-generated images, video or audio. The Moon on the page and in the slides is NASA imagery drawn by code. The demo video is screenshots of the page joined by a script the tool wrote, and its last card says so. We use no NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
